title: A mirror for meditation
hookLine: the lists as a mirror: seeing which factors are present while sitting

cards: A father and his young son. The boy is Rahula, and the father is the Buddha. In one of the Majjhima suttas, the Buddha holds up the kind of question you'd ask a child: what is a mirror for?
Rahula gives the plain answer. For looking at yourself. For seeing what's there.
It's one image among several in that talk, and it hands this path a tool for the end of a long block of lists. All those factors, the restless ones, the bright ones, the dull ones: what are they for?

teach.h: BEFORE, WHILE, AND AFTER YOU ACT.
teach.b: First, the mirror in the sutta. After Rahula answers, the Buddha says, in paraphrase: in the same way, look at what you do. Before you act, while you act, and after, reflect on it.
Is this leading to harm, for me or for anyone else? If it is, set it down. If it isn't, carry on, glad.

A mirror is for checking, the way you'd check your face before you walk out the door. Second, the mirror while sitting. In the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness, one thing a meditator watches is the mind itself.

teach.h: A MIND WITH GREED, KNOWN AS SUCH.
teach.b: In paraphrase: a mind with greed is known as a mind with greed; a mind without it is known as a mind without it. The same with anger, with confusion, with a mind that's scattered or gathered. Nothing is added.

teach.h: THE LISTS GIVE THE GLASS EDGES.
teach.b: You just see what's in the glass. Third, what the lists add. The suttas give the outline; the Abhidhamma fills in the detail: restlessness, doubt, sloth, envy; mindfulness, calm, softness, compassion.
When you sit, those names can work like the edges of a mirror. Something stirs, and instead of a fog you can say: oh, that's restlessness. That's doubt.
That's a small moment of calm. Fourth, what a mirror never does.
It doesn't scold, and it doesn't flatter. It shows a smudge on your cheek the same way it shows your smile. Some teachers of this practice stress that the naming is for seeing, not for grading.
A factor in the glass isn't a verdict on you. It's what's there this moment, and the next moment may show something else.

how: In insight meditation, some Theravada teachers have students note what arises in the mind with a soft label, such as restless or calm, and then return to the breath or the body.

games.q: what does “a mirror for meditation” mean?
o: naming the mind's factors to see, not to grade
a mirror set up beside a shrine to the Buddha
a way to judge whether you're a good person

p: asked what a mirror is for
when to reflect on what you do
known as a mind with greed
names that give the mirror its edges

s: naming a factor while sitting is a way of grading yourself
the naming is for seeing, not for grading. a mirror shows a smudge and a smile the same way.
in the sutta, the Buddha uses a mirror to teach his son
he asks Rahula what a mirror is for, then says to reflect before, during and after acting.
the meditator watching the mind tries to add something to what's there
a mind with greed is known as a mind with greed. nothing is added.

games.q: you're sitting, and restlessness shows up. what does the mirror ask of you?
o: push it away until it's gone
name it quietly and come back
games.why: a mirror shows and doesn't scold: one soft name, restless, and back to the breath. the next moment may show something else.

practice: Let the breath go at its own pace, and when something shows up in the mind, give it one quiet name, the way you'd read a label: restless, tired, curious, doubt, calm. Don't chase it away or hold on to it.
If no name fits, just say, something, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: A mirror for meditation. The lists of mental factors used the way the Buddha told Rahula to use a mirror: to see what's there, without scolding. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a mirror. It shows the smudge and the smile the same way, and it never scolds. Same time tomorrow.
